prompt: Some people believe every student should be required to spend a set number of hours each year volunteering in their community. Others believe that help given because it is required is not really help at all, and that students should choose for themselves whether and when to serve. Do you agree that community service should be required of students? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response takes a clear position in the opening and holds it, rather than listing the good and bad points and stopping. Development matters more than range: two examples explored closely — what happened, what it showed — will outscore five named in passing. The best responses also acknowledge the opposing view honestly and explain why it does not change the writer's mind.
accessibility_note: A student whose school has never organized volunteering may have no direct experience to draw on, but the prompt explicitly invites examples from reading or observation, so a candidate can argue from a family member's work, a news story, or a club they have watched from outside.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "The bus took a turn it had never taken before, and no one else on it seemed to notice."
guidance: A strong story does one small thing well rather than sketching an entire plot; in twenty-five minutes, a single scene with a real ending beats a summary of an adventure. Look for concrete detail — what the narrator sees, hears, decides — and for a narrator whose reaction to the strangeness tells us who they are. The opening sentence should be used, not abandoned after the first paragraph.
accessibility_note: A student who has never ridden a city bus may hesitate at the setting, but the situation only requires imagining an ordinary journey going slightly wrong, which any reader of the sentence can picture from the sentence itself.

prompt: Some people say it is better to pick one activity and get truly good at it. Others say the years when you are young are exactly the time to try many things, even if you never become excellent at any of them. Which do you think is the better way to spend your time, and why? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response defines what it means by "better" early — better for skill, for happiness, for later choices — because the argument depends on it. Specificity is the difference between an adequate and a strong paper: name the activity, the hours, the moment the writer felt the trade-off. Paragraphs should each do a distinct job rather than restate the introduction in new words.
accessibility_note: A student with few organized activities available to them can still answer from schoolwork, chores, or self-taught interests, since the question is about how attention is spent rather than about access to lessons or teams.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "The dog would not stop barking at the empty chair."
guidance: A strong story resists the temptation to explain the mystery away in the last line; an ending can leave the cause unresolved as long as something in the narrator has changed. Reward writing that grounds the scene in physical detail — the room, the time of day, who else is present — instead of relying on atmosphere alone. Dialogue, if used, should sound like the people speaking it.
accessibility_note: A student who has never lived with a pet is not disadvantaged, because the sentence supplies everything needed: an animal insisting on something the humans cannot see.

prompt: When a school team or club has more people who want to join than it has places, some believe places should go to those with the most ability, so the group can do its best work. Others believe anyone willing to work hard should be allowed to take part, even if the group's results suffer. Which approach should a school choose? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response engages with the cost of its own position rather than pretending there is none, and the strongest name what is lost and argue it is worth losing. Organization should be visible: a reader ought to be able to state the writer's reason for each paragraph after one reading. Examples should be particular cases, not general claims about "most students."
accessibility_note: A student at a school with no selective teams may not have watched cuts happen, but the same tension appears in class projects, group assignments, and any shared space with limited room, all of which are fair ground for the argument.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "The vending machine gave back more money than I had put in, and the next day it did it again."
guidance: A strong story lets a small choice carry weight: the interest lies in what the narrator decides to do the second time, not in the machine. Watch for pacing — a candidate who spends the first half describing the hallway will not reach an ending. The best responses show consequence, however quiet, rather than stopping at the moment of temptation.
accessibility_note: The prompt involves money but assumes no particular amount or family circumstance; a student for whom the sum matters greatly and one for whom it does not can each write a strong story, since the question is about the choice, not the wealth.

prompt: When something we own breaks, we can repair it or replace it. Some people believe repairing is almost always the better choice, for what it teaches and what it saves. Others believe that time and effort are worth more than the object, and that replacing frees us to move on. Do you agree that it is better to repair than to replace? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response resists treating this as a question with an obvious answer and tests its position against a hard case — something not worth repairing, or something worth repairing at absurd cost. Transitions should carry the argument forward rather than merely signal a new paragraph. Concrete objects, named and described, will do more work here than abstract statements about waste.
accessibility_note: A student may read this as a question about money and answer from that angle, or as a question about attachment and answer from that one; both readings are legitimate and neither requires owning anything expensive.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "The letter was addressed to someone who had lived in our apartment before us."
guidance: A strong story keeps its scope tight — one afternoon, one decision about the letter — and earns its ending rather than announcing it. Look for a narrator with a clear voice and a reason to care, and for detail that suggests the absent person without stating their whole history. Whether the letter is opened matters less than whether the writer has thought about why.
accessibility_note: A student who has always lived in one home can still write this, since the premise supplies the situation entirely; no experience of moving, and no particular kind of household, is required.

prompt: Some students learn best when they work through a problem alone; others learn best when they work it through with a group. Which way of working teaches you more, and why? Use examples from your own schoolwork or activities to support your position.
guidance: A strong response takes a clear position in the opening paragraph and holds it, rather than drifting between the two options or ending in "both are good." It should develop two or three distinct reasons, each anchored in a specific remembered situation — a particular assignment, rehearsal, or study session — rather than general claims about students. The best essays acknowledge what the other way of working offers and explain why it still matters less to the writer.
accessibility_note: A student who has mostly studied alone may feel they lack group experience, but the prompt asks which teaches them more, and a well-argued preference built on their own solitary work is fully creditable.

prompt: Think of a time you changed your mind about something you had believed or an opinion you had held. What made you change it, and how did you feel afterward? Explain what the experience taught you about your own thinking.
guidance: A strong response narrows to a single, concrete change of mind and gives the reader enough of the before and after to see the shift actually happen. Look for reflection that goes past "I learned to listen" — the strongest essays name what specifically moved them (a fact, a person's situation, an experience) and are honest about whether changing felt like relief, embarrassment, or both. Chronological order works well here as long as the reflection is developed, not tacked on in a final sentence.
accessibility_note: A student who cannot recall a dramatic reversal may worry their example is too small; an ordinary change of opinion about a person, a subject, or a habit is exactly what this prompt invites.

prompt: Some people believe that games and sports for young children should be played without keeping score, so that everyone can enjoy taking part. Others believe keeping score teaches children how to win and lose honestly. Which view do you agree with, and why?
guidance: A strong response states its position early and defends it with reasons about children specifically, not just about the writer's own taste for competition. Development matters more than range here: two well-explained reasons, each with an example of how a scored or unscored game actually plays out, beat a list of five assertions. Responses that fairly represent the opposing view before answering it tend to read as the most mature.
accessibility_note: A student who does not play organized sports can argue equally well from board games, classroom contests, or watching younger siblings, since the prompt is about children and competition rather than athletic skill.

prompt: Messages, calls, and posts let people stay in constant contact with friends who are far away. Some people think this makes friendships stronger; others think it makes the friendships closest to us weaker, because our attention is somewhere else. What do you think, and why?
guidance: A strong response defines what it means by a stronger or weaker friendship early on, so the argument has something to measure against. The best essays reason from observed behavior — how a conversation goes, what someone does at a lunch table — rather than repeating familiar complaints about screens. A clear structure with each paragraph carrying one idea will do more for the score than a dramatic conclusion.
accessibility_note: A student with limited access to a phone or the internet can write from what they observe in others, and their outside perspective often produces sharper evidence than a heavy user's.

prompt: When a group needs a leader, some people look for the person who speaks up first and decides quickly. Others look for the person who listens longest before saying anything. Which of these makes the better leader, and why? Support your answer with examples.
guidance: A strong response resists the temptation to praise both kinds equally and instead argues for one, ideally by naming the conditions under which that leader succeeds. Examples drawn from a class project, a team, a club, or a family decision are more persuasive than examples drawn from famous figures the writer knows only at a distance. Watch for an essay that develops a real counterargument — the decisive leader's speed, or the listener's patience — and answers it directly.
accessibility_note: A student who has never held a formal leadership title can write from being led, since judging leaders from inside a group is a legitimate and often more revealing vantage point.

prompt: Imagine your community has one empty lot and enough money to build only one thing on it: a small park or a small library. Which should it build, and why? Explain your reasoning to someone who lives there and disagrees with you.
guidance: A strong response keeps its audience in view — the neighbor who disagrees — and therefore argues rather than merely asserts, granting what the other choice offers before explaining why it loses. Specificity about who benefits and how often is what separates a developed essay from a general one. A conclusion that restates the choice in light of the reasoning, instead of repeating the opening sentence, is a good sign.
accessibility_note: A student whose neighborhood has neither a park nor a library can reason from what its absence costs, and that argument is as valid as one drawn from having both.

prompt: Some people plan their days carefully and follow the plan. Others leave their time open and decide as they go. Which approach do you think leads to a better use of a day, and why? Draw on your own experience in your answer.
guidance: A strong response commits to one approach and shows its cost as well as its benefit, since the honest essay here admits what is lost either way. Concrete accounts of particular days — a Saturday, an exam week, a holiday — develop the argument far better than general statements about organization. Clear paragraphing and transitions matter especially in this prompt, because the two approaches are easy to blur together.
accessibility_note: A student whose time is largely arranged by family or work obligations can write about the narrow part of the day that is theirs to shape, and that constraint often yields the most thoughtful response.

prompt: Describe a place you can reach on foot that matters to you. Explain what happens there, and why it holds the importance it does. Help a reader who has never been there understand why it is worth describing.
guidance: A strong response chooses a single place and grounds it in sensory, specific detail rather than a tour of several locations. The organization should serve the point: description exists to explain the importance, so an essay that lingers on appearance without ever saying why it matters is underdeveloped, and one that asserts importance without any concrete detail is thin. The best responses let the significance emerge from a moment that happened there.
accessibility_note: By limiting the place to walking distance, the prompt makes no assumption about travel or resources, and a stairwell, a bus stop, or a corner of a room can be written about as powerfully as anywhere else.
